♻ ☆ Scaling Verifiable Environments for Long-horizon Work Agents
Jiazheng Zhang, Long Ma, Yunxian Yang, Zhiheng Xi, Zhikai Lei, Yajie Yang, Chenyang Liao, Enyu Zhou, Yang Nan, Yuchen Tian, Senjie Jin, Yibo Wang, Wei He, Boyang Liu, Jixuan Huang, Xin Guo, Shutong Jiang, Zhezheng Hao, Xinbing Liang, Zhihao Zhang, Changzhi Zhou, Wiggin Zhou, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Clarenceai
Work agents operate over digital artifacts to execute professional knowledge-intensive work, requiring training environments that support long-horizon interaction and trustworthy verification. However, hand-crafted environments incur prohibitive engineering overhead that prevents environment scaling, whereas synthesis methods sacrifice workspace complexity, realism, or grounded verifiability. To bridge this gap, we introduce WorkForge, a scalable synthesis framework for constructing verifiable work-agent environments from real-world resources. Starting from expert workflows, WorkForge first identifies the resources, decisions, and deliverables required by each workflow. It then retrieves relevant real-world files and organizes them into a workspace. WorkForge inspects the workspace to extract concrete, checkable facts about its content. These factual anchors fix which task types the workspace can support and how their outcomes can be verified. Therefore, WorkForge derives each task's instructions, solution plan, and complementary programmatic and semantic verifiers directly from these factual anchors, keeping verification traceable to observable workspace evidence. Furthermore, we construct 16.7K verifiable environments across 40 professional domains, with workspaces collectively covering 60 file types. Post-training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base improves GDPVal from 45.5 to 73.6 and APEX Score from 5.0 to 21.3, while enabling Qwen3.5-27B to achieve highly competitive performance and outperform strong competitors. Our analyses confirm the efficacy of the proposed method and reveal consistent scaling behaviors across both data volume and interaction horizons.
♻ ☆ SAPO: Single-Rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Dayang Liang, Lang Feng, Bo An, Yunlong Liu
Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as an important post-training approach for enhancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods face a trade-off between policy performance and resource efficiency. Conventional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) implementations incur substantial memory overhead from a separate critic, whereas critic-free group-relative methods require multiple rollouts and face potential learning bottlenecks on long-horizon tasks. In this work, we propose Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO), an efficient PPO-style framework that unifies policy optimization and value learning within a single causal language model. SAPO exploits the autoregressive structure of LLMs to sequentially generate action and value estimation at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, and then jointly optimizes the PPO objectives and an auxiliary on-policy SARSA objective with turn-level generalized advantage estimation, where the latter is designed to facilitate value learning. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-14B demonstrate that SAPO reduces peak GPU memory usage by 24.8% and per-iteration runtime by 23.1% over strong PPO baseline, while matching or slightly improving task success rate. Our experiments also show that SAPO outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and recent cutting-edge variants in both task success and training stability.

♻ ☆ Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning
Samuel Barbeau, Simon Roy, Giovanni Beltrame, Christian Desrosiers, Nicolas Thome
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable agents to plan in latent space by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, yet task specification remains a bottleneck. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on distinct large generative models. We introduce LAGO (Latent Goal Prediction from Language), a hierarchical world model in which a single predictor both forecasts action-conditioned dynamics and grounds language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, training both modes with a single regression objective over a shared latent space. At each planning step, LAGO predicts a sequence of latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes an action sequence using a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path. Subgoals are repredicted as the agent's state evolves, turning a single long-horizon instruction into a sequence of locally tractable objectives. Across environments spanning navigation and manipulation, LAGO outperforms flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation with curved, hazard-constrained paths, where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy trained on the same demonstrations. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space also outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that plans with ground-truth dynamics.

♻ ☆ Missingness-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Fusion for Human Activity Recognition from Low-Quality Wearable Sensor Data
Jiangtao Fan, Anish Jindal, Amir Atapour-Abarghouei
Body-worn sensor networks capture human activities through complementary views, where nodes, modalities, and axes partially describe the underlying motion. In real deployments, hardware faults, wireless dropouts, and loose attachments often cause entire channels or nodes to go missing, while environmental interference degrades the remaining signals. The common impute-then-recognize pipeline introduces reconstruction errors that cannot be observed or corrected at inference. We propose the Missingness-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Network (MCSTN), an end-to-end framework for robust activity recognition under imperfect sensing. MCSTN has three components: a structured imperfection generator that simulates point, temporal-block, axis, modality, and node failures, plus noise at varying signal-to-noise levels; a mask-aware representation that conditions node embeddings, attention, and temporal aggregation on the availability mask; and a complete-to-imperfect multi-view learning scheme where an exponential-moving-average teacher guides multiple degraded student views through semantic consistency. The encoder models temporal and cross-feature dependencies in parallel: a bi-directional selective state-space branch captures long-range temporal dependencies, a transposed-attention branch models cross-channel correlations, and adaptive weights fuse their outputs. At inference, the generator, teacher, and consistency loss are removed, so MCSTN predicts directly from the observed window and its mask without reconstruction or noise-level estimation. On PAMAP2, Opportunity, and WISDM, MCSTN achieves average macro-F1 scores of 94.24\%, 91.67\%, and 96.22\% under imperfect observations, the best among all compared methods on each dataset, and the best in every failure mode on Opportunity. It requires fewer than one million parameters, with 3.78~ms inference latency per sample.
♻ ☆ Enhancing Software Engineering Through Closed-Loop Memory Optimization
Xuehang Guo, Xingyao Wang, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Qingyun Wang, Graham Neubig, Heng Ji
Large language models (LLMs) have enabled powerful software engineering (SE) agents capable of navigating complex codebases and resolving real-world issues. However, these agents remain fundamentally episodic: they fail to retain, refine, and reuse experiences across tasks, repeatedly reconstructing context from scratch and reproducing similar mistakes. Even with memory support, they offer no remedy for the absence of a principled, task-agnostic \textit{memory utility}, making them difficult to evaluate rigorously or generalize across agents and settings. To tackle these limitations, we introduce MemOp, a closed-loop framework for memory augmentation in SE agents. MemOp grounds memory utility in \textit{validated downstream impact}, establishing utility as both a task-agnostic \textbf{evaluation benchmark} and an annotation-free \textbf{optimization signal}. Evaluating MemOp across four benchmarks, three programming languages, and two SE agents, under complementary \textit{single-episode} and \textit{cross-episode} memory augmentation, results demonstrate the \textbf{effectiveness} of MemOp, achieving absolute gains of up to $\uparrow5.25\%$ in success rate and $\uparrow4.63\%$ in resolve efficiency, while notably reducing deployment cost by $\geq10.33\%$. MemOp further exhibits \textbf{generalizability} across SE agents, memory backbones, and optimization algorithms, together with \textbf{transferability} of MemOp-trained memory model to unseen programming languages and SE activities. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/MemOp/.
♻ ☆ Learning Scenario Reduction for Two-Stage Robust Optimization with Discrete Uncertainty NeurIPS 2026
Tianjue Lin, Jianan Zhou, Jieyi Bi, Yaoxin Wu, Wen Song, Zhiguang Cao, Jie Zhang
Two-Stage Robust Optimization (2RO) with discrete uncertainty is challenging, often rendering exact solutions prohibitive. Scenario reduction alleviates this issue by selecting a small, representative subset of scenarios to enable tractable computation. However, existing methods are largely problem-agnostic, operating solely on the uncertainty set without consulting the feasible region or recourse structure. In this paper, we introduce PRISE, a problem-driven sequential lookahead heuristic that constructs reduced scenario sets by evaluating the marginal impact of each scenario. While PRISE yields high-quality scenario subsets, each selection step requires solving multiple subproblems, making it computationally expensive at scale. To address this, we propose NeurPRISE, a neural surrogate model built on a GNN-Transformer backbone that encodes the per-scenario structure via graph convolution and captures cross-scenario interactions through attention. NeurPRISE is trained via imitation learning with a gain-aware ranking objective, which distills marginal gain information from PRISE into a learned scoring function for scenario ranking and selection. Extensive results on three 2RO problems show that NeurPRISE consistently achieves competitive regret relative to comprehensive methods, maintains strong calability with varying numbers of scenarios, and delivers 17-200x speedup over PRISE. NeurPRISE also exhibits strong zero-shot generalization, effectively handling instances with larger problem scales (up to 5x), more scenarios (up to 4x), and distribution shifts.

♻ ☆ Learning Faithful Reasoning Processes with Spatio-Temporal Latent Dynamics for Large Language Models
Weijiang Lv, Wentong Zhao, Jiayu Wang, Yuhao Wu, Jiaheng Wei, Xiaobo Xia
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing reinforcement learning methods primarily optimize outcome-level rewards, providing limited supervision over the reasoning process. As a result, models may produce shortcut-prone or unstable reasoning trajectories even when the final answer is correct. We propose GeoFaith, a spatio-temporal latent dynamics framework for learning faithful reasoning processes without process reward models. GeoFaith combines final-state latent uncertainty, which measures whether a completed trajectory lies in a well-supported manifold region, with predictive-entropy dynamics, which penalize abnormal uncertainty patterns such as premature collapse, oscillation, and prolonged uncertainty. These signals are incorporated as process regularization into GRPO, jointly optimizing answer correctness and reasoning quality without step-level process annotations. Experiments show that GeoFaith consistently improves reasoning accuracy, produces more efficient reasoning trajectories, and outperforms both outcome-only reinforcement learning and process-supervision baselines.
♻ ☆ Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search ICML 2026
Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Groezinger, Maximilian Forstenhäusler, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Pierpaolo Mori, Nael Fasfous, Alexander Frickenstein, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.7 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 19%. ♻ ☆ EpiFlow: Bridging Safety and Performance in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Guided Flow Matching NeurIPS 2026
Manan Tayal, Mumuksh Tayal, Ravi Prakash
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising framework for deploying autonomous systems in safety-critical settings without the risks of online exploration. However, learning policies that simultaneously achieve high performance and strong safety guarantees from fixed datasets remains a fundamental challenge. Many existing safe offline RL approaches typically rely on soft constraint formulations, which may permit safety violations and are sensitive to distributional shift. In contrast, formal methods such as Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide rigorous safety guarantees, but often yield overly conservative solutions, often neglecting performance. In this work, we bridge this gap by formulating safe offline RL as a state-constrained optimal control problem, where safety is enforced through hard state constraints and performance is captured via a reward function. The resulting value function satisfies a Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, which we approximate using offline RL on fixed datasets by learning an epigraph feasibility value function and extracting policies via flow matching. This formulation enables principled integration of safety guarantees with data-driven policy optimization. Empirically, across safety-critical benchmarks including boat navigation, Safety-Gymnasium, and Bullet-Safety-Gym tasks, our approach achieves competitive returns while exhibiting near-zero constraint violations, demonstrating a favorable balance between safety and performance in the offline setting.

♻ ★ Learning Loco-Manipulation From SMPC Demonstrations With Sparse Offline-to-Online RL CoRL 2026
Martin Schuck, Maks Sorokin, Simone Manni, Duy Ta, Angela P. Schoellig, Marco Hutter, Simon Le Cleac'H, Jan Brüdigam
Integrating locomotion and manipulation is essential for robot autonomy, but scaling standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) to complex tasks is severely bottlenecked by the slow, manual process of dense reward shaping. To bypass this limitation, we leverage Sample-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) entirely in simulation as an automated, rapidly tunable expert to generate massive offline datasets. Because this data solves the fundamental exploration problem, we can train an off-policy RL agent using purely sparse task rewards, drastically reducing the time required to learn new skills and eliminating the need for manual tuning. Integrating this high-level agent with a low-level dynamic stability controller yields more optimal behaviors that strictly align with true task objectives, ultimately allowing the learned policies to surpass the original optimal control teacher. We validate the robustness of this sim-to-real framework by successfully deploying complex loco-manipulation skills across different morphologies, including an arm-equipped Spot quadruped and a G1 humanoid.

♻ ☆ What Makes Synthetic Hard Negatives Work in Vision-Language Pretraining? ACCV 2026
Nikos Giakoumoglou, Paschalis Giakoumoglou, Andreas Floros, Kleanthis Marios Papadopoulos, Tania Stathaki
Synthetic hard negatives generated in the representation space have proven effective for unimodal self-supervised learning, but transferring this idea to vision-language pretraining is not straightforward. We analyze six representation-space synthesis strategies and identify two failure modes in their transfer to vision-language pretraining: cross-modal constructions that produce overly easy negatives or pull them toward the query, and intra-modal constructions that incorporate the matched positive. We also observe logit-scale saturation when training with synthetic hard negatives and a learnable temperature, and find that fixing the temperature improves downstream performance. Using this geometric analysis we propose SNAP, which generates intra-modal hard negatives that never involve the positive from either modality, avoiding both failure modes entirely. SNAP is model-agnostic, requires no external generative models, and adds less than 10% training time overhead. Evaluated on top of CLIP and FLIP across multiple architectures and datasets, SNAP delivers consistent improvements on zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probe evaluation.

Wearable devices provide continuous access to physiological signals such as ECG and PPG, offering a path to answering users' questions about their own physiological state and to early detection of cardiac and physiological abnormalities. Yet existing mobile health (mHealth) systems are largely limited to task-specific prediction pipelines or reactive question answering over static summaries. To advance this setting, we introduce VitalBench, a longitudinal physiological monitoring benchmark comprising 1,862 QA pairs for reactive question answering and 90.2 hours of continuous ECG/PPG recordings for proactive monitoring, covering cardiac, physical activity, and stress-related tasks. VitalAgent is built on a longitudinal physiological memory and a tool-augmented reasoning interface that enables dynamic computation over raw signals. Experiments demonstrate that VitalAgent achieves over 25 points absolute improvement over prompt-based and agentic baselines in reactive evaluation and enables proactive alert monitoring over long-term physiological signals, pointing toward mHealth systems that can both answer questions about and continuously monitor a person's physiological state beyond the clinic.

♻ ☆ Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs
Bo Liu, Tong Li, Jiapeng Zhang, Zhu Xiao, Zhuo Tang, Kenli Li
Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.

Real-world experiments show Crazyflow supports both analytical-gradient-based policy learning, achieving high-accuracy tracking without domain randomization, and sampling-based obstacle avoidance at speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second. ♻ ☆ CausalMix: Data Mixture as Causal Inference for Language Model Training NeurIPS 2026
Zinan Tang, Yukun Zhang, Shaomian Zheng, Zhuoshi Pan, Qizhi Pei, Dingnan Jin, Qing Cui, Jun Zhou, Yujun Wang, Biqing Huang
In Large Language Model (LLM) training, data mixing plays a pivotal role in determining model performance. Recent methods optimize mixture weights via proxy models, but they rely on the assumption of static data distributions. As a result, when the underlying data pool shifts, these methods require costly retraining from scratch. This limitation restricts their ability to scale seamlessly from small settings to larger data pools and model sizes. In this paper, we propose CausalMix to address this limitation by casting data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem. We formulate the statistical features of the data pool as covariates and the domain mixture as the treatment. After fitting a causal model on 512 runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), we extrapolate the optimal mixture for an 800K data pool and apply it to train a 7B model. Furthermore, we successfully generalize the framework to long chain-of-thought data on Qwen3-4B-Base. By leveraging causal modeling to isolate confounding biases, CausalMix infers state-dependent data mixtures offline, with the selected mixture fixed during each training run. Extensive experiments show that the mixture guided by CausalMix achieves competitive performance across downstream tasks compared with other baselines. The CATE Interpreter visualizes the learned mixing strategy. Overall, CausalMix offers a causal and interpretable framework for optimizing LLM data mixtures.

Optimization and Control 73
★ Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
Adam Quinn Jaffe, Congwei Yang, Nicolás García Trillos, Bodhisattva Sen
While the goal of classical statistical theory is to minimize the variance of unbiased estimators, an additional goal of some recent research is to minimize or constrain other notions of the instability of estimators. In particular, a subset of the authors recently introduced a notion of instability termed "sensitivity", which represents the expected amount that an estimator would change if its inputs were infinitesimally perturbed. In this work, we study the multiobjective problem of minimizing both the variance and sensitivity over unbiased estimators in a given statistical model, and we aim to determine Pareto optimal tradeoffs between these two objectives. Our main results show that the Pareto front for these tradeoffs is precisely determined by endowing the statistical model with the Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry, which interpolates between the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries that are known to be associated, respectively, with the separate minimization of variance and sensitivity. We also develop a $Z$-estimation technique which constructs estimators that asymptotically achieve Pareto optimal pairs of variance and sensitivity. While computing the Pareto front and constructing the resulting estimators in practice requires solving a continuum of partial differential equations, we fully execute this program in some parametric examples of interest where the analysis is already non-trivial. Our results also shed light on some classical statistical problems, for example by showing that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves the smallest asymptotic sensitivity among all estimators achieving the optimal asymptotic variance.

☆ Data-Driven Stochastic Control of Delayed Air-Conditioning Systems
Christian Bayer, Raul Tempone, Leon Wilkosz
We consider a stochastic optimal control problem arising in the operation of industrial air-conditioning systems with delayed activation effects. The delayed transition between inactive and operational regimes induces a non-Markovian structure in the controlled dynamics. We derive a regression-based discrete dynamic programming algorithm on nested state-control grids. We give a probabilistic proof of convergence of the idealized time-discrete dynamic programming problem to the continuous-time value function. Numerical experiments based on calibrated multidimensional forecast-tracking Ornstein--Uhlenbeck models illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.
☆ A Stochastic Proximal-Gradient Method for Regularized Generally Constrained Continuous Optimization
Frank E. Curtis, Xiaoyi Qu, Daniel P. Robinson
A stochastic proximal-gradient method is proposed and analyzed for solving regularized optimization problems subject to nonlinear equality constraints and nonnegativity bounds. The objective function's values and gradients are available only through inexact stochastic oracles. The method decomposes each trial step into one component that reduces linearized infeasibility and a second component that seeks optimality while preserving that reduction. Trial steps are accepted or rejected through a relaxed sufficient decrease condition subject to stochastic merit function evaluations. Without assuming unbiasedness of stochastic gradient estimates, it is proved under reasonable assumptions that the method reaches an $ε$-KKT point within $O(ε^{-2})$ iterations with high probability. This guarantee further implies almost-sure termination in finitely many iterations and an $O(ε^{-2})$ bound on the expected iteration complexity.
☆ Learning Behavioral Parameters of Network Equilibrium Models from Aggregate Mobility Data
Tenglong Hong, Youngseo Kim
Estimating travel behavior parameters is essential for understanding current travel patterns and for forecasting how travelers may respond to future changes in transportation systems. However, reliable estimation remains difficult when behavior must be inferred from sparse and aggregate observations, especially when jointly recovering several behavioral components. In this paper, we develop a bi-level estimation program for a combined destination, mode and route choice model with congestion. The inner level is a convex program at given scale parameters, and returns the taste coefficients as its dual variables together with the equilibrium travel pattern. The outer level selects the scale parameters by out-of-sample prediction, measured by how well the modeled travel pattern predicts observations withheld from estimation. ☆ Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control via Trajectory Optimization

The curse of dimensionality associated with solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function remains a key obstacle for real-time optimal feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. This is especially severe in aerospace applications such as relaminarizing unsteady turbulent flows and recovering from aerodynamic stall where nonlinear dynamics play a significant role. We introduce Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control (BASOC), a model reduction framework which seeks to find directions in state space along which the value function is most sensitive, and the distribution of states exhibits maximum variance along optimal trajectories. BASOC leverages trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to obtain state and co-state (value function gradient) data along locally optimal trajectories for constructing state and gradient covariance matrices. Balancing these matrices provides an oblique projection for approximating the value function, which can also be used to construct reduced-order models and surrogate feedback control laws. We show that for linear-quadratic optimal control problems, BASOC becomes equivalent to a snapshot method for initial condition balancing of the optimally controlled closed-loop realization. The framework is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-dimensional system where POD and balanced truncation are known to perform poorly, and on the nonlinear complex Ginzburg-Landau equation to demonstrate feasibility for larger-scale systems.
☆ AHEAD: Adaptive Neural Acceleration for Large-Scale Linear Programming
Sihao Liu, Zhichao Hou, Huayue Gu, Raiyan Rahman, Liang Wu, Ruozhou Yu, Xiaorui Liu
Large-scale linear programs with millions of variables and constraints strain time and memory budgets. First-order methods such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient scale to this regime because they avoid matrix factorizations, but they require many iterations. Learned accelerators can reduce these iterations, yet fewer iterations do not guarantee a shorter solve. Learning inference also takes time, and running the accelerator longer trades solver time for inference time. Existing unrolled accelerators handle this trade-off poorly: each layer processes every variable and constraint, the predicted iterates still need solver refinement, and every instance runs the same layers. We therefore ask: What neural accelerator design achieves end-to-end speedups on large-scale linear programs across sizes and target accuracies? We introduce AHEAD, an accelerator that predicts step sizes for first-order linear programming solvers while keeping their update rules. Its weight-shared predictor reads compact solver statistics and rescales the primal and dual step sizes, so each warm-start iteration stays inexpensive and a short warm-start phase hands the solver a warm start. A learned handoff policy sets the number of warm-start iterations for each instance and target accuracy, after which the solver finishes under its own termination criterion. On packing linear programs with up to $10^7$ variables, AHEAD achieves $6.5$--$11.6\times$ end-to-end speedups over Gurobi's first-order solver from a cold start, including on instances of unseen sizes and distributions. The gains extend to PageRank linear programs and hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.
☆ A unified family of multiblock ADMM schemes by means of graph splitting
Rubén Campoy, Scott B. Lindstrom, César López-Pastor
This paper introduces a novel unified family of multiblock ADMM schemes by combining Gabay duality with a graph-based splitting methodology. This framework allows us to recover existing ADMM algorithms as particular instances, as well as to generate new ones by varying the underlying network topology. We focus specifically on the case of the complete graph, a structure of significant practical interest due to its dense connectivity, for which we provide a fully explicit and directly implementable scheme. We further derive an equivalent reformulation of the proposed family in which the algorithm is expressed in terms of a reduced set of dual variables, which clarifies its connection to the classical ADMM framework. Numerical experiments are conducted to compare the performance of different graph choices, showing particularly favorable results for the complete graph.
☆ Proximal Point Newton Methods for Nonconvex Optimization
Chang He, Shuzhong Zhang
Tensor methods offer improved complexity guarantees for nonconvex optimization, but evaluating high-order derivatives and solving the corresponding subproblems can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we develop a proximal point Newton framework that exploits third-derivative smoothness using only gradients and Hessians. Under Hessian Lipschitz continuity, a single-loop proximal point Newton method that alternates between negative-curvature directions and Newton steps finds an $(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)$-approximate second-order stationary point within $\mathcal{O}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-3/2},\varepsilon_H^{-3}\})$ second-order oracle evaluations. When the third derivative is also Lipschitz continuous, we introduce an accelerated proximal point Newton method and obtain a dimension-free complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-4/3},\varepsilon_H^{-2}\})$, matching that of the third-order tensor methods up to logarithmic factors without constructing tensors or solving tensor subproblems. We further develop an adaptive inexact Newton--CG variant that requires no prior knowledge of Lipschitz constants and preserves the improved oracle complexity with high probability. Under uniformly bounded queried Hessians, this variant achieves a Hessian-vector product complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-5/3},\varepsilon_H^{-5/2}\})$, improving upon the previous $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-3}\varepsilon_H^{5/2},\varepsilon_H^{-7/2}\})$ result attained by existing second-order methods such as cubic regularized Newton method and Newton--CG method. Preliminary numerical experiments are encouraging.
☆ Cost benefits of designing carbon capture processes for part-load operation of power plants
David Yang Shu, Boxun Huang, Yurim Kim, Rahul Gandhi, Randall Field, Sungho Shin
As fossil power plants increasingly cycle to balance variable renewable generation, carbon capture plants must be designed for a wide range of part-load operating conditions, to avoid excessive capital costs. However, accounting for the variability in design optimization yields higher computational complexity, and is therefore not a current design methodology. Here, we apply two-stage stochastic optimization to identify optimal carbon capture plant designs accounting for part-load flue gas conditions. We reduce computational complexity through a data-driven approach-to-equilibrium model of the absorption and desorption processes. Operating scenarios are derived from real-world part-load operation data of coal and natural gas combined cycle power plants. Our results demonstrate that designs optimized over multiple operating scenarios substantially reduce equipment sizes, lowering capital costs by 5-9 % at the expense of higher operating costs, resulting in a moderate reduction in total annualized cost by 0.5-1.6 %. The lowest costs are achieved when targeting an average capture target across operating scenarios, which allows CO2 capture to be shifted from full-load to part-load periods to reduce peak equipment sizes without compromising overall CO2 emission reductions. These cost benefits are robust across sensitivity analyses and increase with higher shares of part-load operation. Thus, part-load variability should be considered at the design stage, particularly for plants subject to variable load.
comment: 32 pages, 11 figures
☆ Stability of Doubly Indexed Discrete Linear Systems
Alain Bourget, Tyler McMillen
We study the stability of the two-dimensional discrete dynamical system defined by \[ x_{i,j} = A x_{i-1,j} + B x_{i,j-1},\] where $A, B \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$. Although this system, commonly known as the Fornasini-Marchesini model, has been examined for decades, several key stability results have lacked rigorous proofs. This paper establishes precise and self-contained criteria for Lyapunov, asymptotic, and neutral stability under general bounded boundary conditions. In particular, we prove that asymptotic stability is equivalent to the spectral condition $ ρ(z_1 A + z_2 B) < 1 $ for all $ |z_1| \leq 1, |z_2| \leq 1 $. We further analyze the commutative case, derive recurrence relations for anti-diagonal sums, and present new examples and counterexamples illustrating the nuances of stability. The results are complemented by sufficient conditions based on matrix norms, Lyapunov functions, and the joint spectral radius.
☆ Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Bounds for Online Linear Optimisation on $\ell_p$ Balls
Jack J. Mayo
We study full-information online linear optimisation on the unit $\ell_p$ ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, for fixed $2\le p<\infty$ and losses of dual norm at most one. Let $Δ_T$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed action above each round's minimum. A follow-the-regularised-leader (FTRL) algorithm attains, on every loss sequence and without knowing $T$ or $Δ_T$, regret $O_p(1+\min\{Δ_T^{1-1/p},\, d^{1/2-1/p}\sqrt{Δ_T}\})$. Matching lower bounds show that this rate is minimax for each fixed $p$, and its constant $(2+o(1))p/\log p$ is optimal as $p\to\infty$ among guarantees uniform in $d$ and $T$. The algorithm uses a bounded radial regulariser and switches at most once to its quadratic augmentation. On some paths where follow-the-leader (FTL) has regret one, its regret grows with $T$. A switching extension keeps the sharp constant and also guarantees $\mathrm{Reg}_T\le 2\,\mathrm{Reg}_T^{\mathrm{FTL}}$. For i.i.d. losses whose mean has no zero coordinates, we compute the exact $\log T$ coefficient of the expected regret, which separates FTL's variance term from the bias of the regulariser.
comment: 49 pages
☆ A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts
Zhen-Fan Wang, Kai Zhang, Xianping Du, Zhaolong Han, Dai Zhou, Onur Bilgen
Wind farm layout optimization becomes increasingly difficult as turbine count grows, especially when high-fidelity aerodynamic models are used. Conventional Kriging-based Bayesian optimization often suffers from low sample efficiency in high-dimensional layout spaces because sparse training data provide limited domain coverage. We develop a Graph-informed Kriging framework that embeds reusable aerodynamic interaction information into the surrogate mean function. The wind farm is represented as a directed aerodynamic graph, where pairwise turbine interactions defined in a low-dimensional relative-coordinate space are assembled into a farm-scale mean. This structured mean captures the dominant variation in annual energy production (AEP), allowing the Gaussian process to model only the residual structure and uncertainty. Numerical experiments show that Graph-informed Kriging consistently improves AEP prediction accuracy over ordinary and generic-trend Kriging under sparse-data conditions, with increasing benefits as layout dimension and wake-interaction strength grow. Embedded in Bayesian optimization, it substantially improves sample efficiency and achieves competitive solutions for the IEA Wind Task 37 benchmark with about 280 AEP evaluations. In a controlled 16-turbine case, it also outperforms ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging under the same high-fidelity evaluation budget. The framework is further extended to a 48-turbine wind farm, demonstrating applicability to large-scale CFD-based layout optimization. These results show that Graph-informed surrogate modeling can enable more efficient use of high-fidelity aerodynamic models for reliable large-scale wind farm layout design.
♻ ☆ Wasserstein-Cramér-Rao Theory of Unbiased Estimation
Nicolás García Trillos, Adam Quinn Jaffe, Bodhisattva Sen
The quantity of interest in the classical Cramér-Rao theory of unbiased estimation (e.g., the Cramér-Rao lower bound, its exact attainment for exponential families, and asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation) is the variance, which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an independently-sampled data set from the same distribution. In this paper we are interested in a quantity which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an infinitesimal additive perturbation of the original data set; we refer to this as the "sensitivity" of an estimator. The resulting theory of sensitivity is based on the Wasserstein geometry in the same way that the classical theory of variance is based on the Fisher-Rao (equivalently, Hellinger) geometry, and this insight allows us to determine a collection of results which are analogous to the classical case: a Wasserstein-Cramér-Rao lower bound for the sensitivity of any unbiased estimator, a characterization of models in which there exist unbiased estimators achieving the lower bound exactly, and various results on the asymptotic achievement of the lower bound. More precisely, we show that Wasserstein projection estimators (and one-step approximations thereof) are asymptotically sensitivity-efficient under suitable assumptions, and that there exist Hodges-type estimators which exhibit super-sensitivity-efficiency. We use these results to treat many statistical examples, sometimes revealing new optimality properties for existing estimators and other times revealing entirely new estimators.
comment: 60 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; comments welcome
♻ ☆ Generalized Wasserstein Flow Matching: Nested Couplings for Point Cloud Generation
Moritz Piening, Richard Duong, Gabriele Steidl
We formulate flow matching on probability measures over probability measures. Directly from the Wasserstein-on-Wasserstein (WoW) continuity equation, we show that admissible nested outer and inner couplings induce a valid metameasure flow and non-local velocity field. Validity requires neither optimal plans nor a smooth manifold. Practically, this opens up the design space of multisample flow matching: exact Wasserstein plans are distinguished by energy and straightness, while sliced and lazy linear plans yield scalable alternatives. Point-cloud experiments, including controlled Bures-Wasserstein and Euclidean minibatch baselines, demonstrate the resulting geometry-cost trade-off.
comment: Keywords: flow matching, Wasserstein over Wasserstein, hierarchical optimal transport, multisample flow matching, minibatch optimal transport, sliced Wasserstein, Bures-Wasserstein, point cloud generation, generative models for distributions, measure-valued data, Wasserstein gradient flow, rectified flow, straight flows
♻ ☆ Online Multi-Level Aggregation with Maximum Delay
Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu, Ke Tang
We study Multi-Level Aggregation with Maximum Delay (MLA-MD) on finite weighted rooted trees. Each service pays for a rooted subtree and for the maximum waiting time among the requests it clears. For the offline problem, we give an exact polynomial-time algorithm that computes both the optimum and an optimal service schedule. For the online problem, we give a deterministic $2$-competitive algorithm and, against an oblivious adversary, a randomized $e/(e-1)$-competitive algorithm. Both competitive ratios are optimal, even on rooted paths. We also extend the offline result and both online guarantees to service systems with submodular costs.
♻ ☆ Analysis of Primal-Dual Langevin Algorithms
Martin Burger, Matthias J. Ehrhardt, Lorenz Kuger, Lukas Weigand
We analyze a recently proposed class of algorithms for the problem of sampling from probability distributions $μ^\ast$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a Lebesgue density of the form $μ^\ast(x) \propto \exp(-f(Kx)-g(x))$, where $K$ is a linear operator and $f,g$ convex and non-smooth. The method is a generalization of the primal-dual hybrid gradient optimization algorithm to a sampling scheme. We give the iteration's continuous time limit, a stochastic differential equation in the joint primal-dual variable, and its mean field limit Fokker-Planck equation. Under mild conditions, the scheme converges to a unique stationary state in continuous and discrete time. Contrary to purely primal overdamped Langevin diffusion, the stationary state in continuous time does not have $μ^\ast$ as its primal marginal. Thus, further analysis is carried out to bound the bias induced by the partial dualization, and potentially correct for it in the diffusion. Time discretizations of the diffusion lead to implementable algorithms, but, as is typical in Langevin Monte Carlo methods, introduce further bias. We prove bounds for these discretization errors, which allow to give convergence results relating the produced samples to the target. We demonstrate our findings numerically first on small-scale examples in which we can exactly verify the theoretical results, and subsequently on typical examples of larger scale from Bayesian imaging inverse problems.
♻ ☆ Variational Analysis of Proximal Compositions and Integral Proximal Mixtures
Patrick L. Combettes, Diego J. Cornejo
This paper establishes various variational properties of parametrized versions of two convexity-preserving constructs that were recently introduced in the literature: the proximal composition of a function and a linear operator, and the integral proximal mixture of arbitrary families of functions and linear operators. We study in particular convexity, Legendre conjugacy, differentiability, Moreau envelopes, coercivity, minimizers, recession functions, and perspective functions of these constructs, as well as their asymptotic behavior as the parameter varies. The special case of the proximal expectation of a family of functions is also discussed.
♻ ☆ Distributed Optimization with Nesterov Momentum and Finite-Time Quantized Averaging over Directed Networks: Extended Version
Ruochen Wu, Xu Du, Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian, Karl H. Johansson, Apostolos I. Rikos
In modern large-scale networked systems, rapidly solving optimization problems while utilizing communication resources efficiently is critical for addressing complex tasks. However, distributed optimization over bandwidth-limited networks must cope with two obstacles: limited-bandwidth communication, and slow convergence when the objective is ill-conditioned. In this paper, we consider unconstrained distributed optimization over strongly connected directed networks, where nodes exchange quantized (i.e., compressed) messages. We propose QANM (Quantized Averaged Nesterov Momentum), an algorithm that combines Nesterov momentum with a finite-time quantized averaging protocol. At every iteration, QANM enables all nodes to reach exact agreement, without requiring doubly stochastic weight matrices or undirected communication. For strongly convex and smooth objectives, we show that the objective gap of QANM decays at the accelerated rate $1-κ^{-1/2}$ (where $κ$ is the condition number), up to a residual of order $Δ^2$ determined by the quantization level $Δ$. This improves the condition-number dependence of the transient iteration complexity from $κ$ to $\sqrtκ$ compared with gradient descent that utilizes the same quantized averaging mechanism. Finally, we evaluate QANM on a distributed sensor fusion problem, showing that our algorithm exhibits the fastest initial error reduction compared with other methods from current literature.
♻ ☆ Mirror descent algorithms with logarithmic barriers
Alberto De Marchi, Yura Malitsky, Adrien B. Taylor
We derive convergence guarantees for mirror descent and proximal mirror descent with a logarithmic barrier as the distance-generating function. When the solution lies on the boundary, the Bregman divergence blows up and classical guarantees become vacuous. While existing remedies recover $O(\log k/k)$ rates by adapting classical bounds, we propose a more direct route in which the Bregman distance to the solution never appears, and which achieves the same rate with constant stepsize. We also construct an example showing that this rate cannot be improved in general. Finally, we compare the proposed approach with interior-point methods.
comment: 18 pages
♻ ☆ Proximal-Linearized NEP Method for Composite Optimization with Set-Inclusion and Manifold Constraints
Hao He, Ruyu Liu, Shaohua Pan
This paper focuses on difference-of-convex (DC) composite optimization problems with set-inclusion and manifold constraints. We develop an inexact proximal-linearized nonsmooth exact penalty (NEP) method that penalizes the conic constraint while retaining the manifold constraint explicitly. At each outer iteration, the method approximately solves a strongly convex proximal-linearized subproblem over the current tangent space, using computable inexactness criteria, adaptive parameters, and a retraction-based acceptance mechanism. Under boundedness of the iterates and penalty parameters, we establish an $O(ε^{-2})$ worst-case outer iteration complexity for finding an $ε$-approximate KKT point of the original problem. We further develop a complexity-transfer framework relating uniform primal objective-gap and KKT-residual decay, or dual objective-gap decay, to total inner-iteration complexity bounds. This yields an $O(ε^{-4})$ overall oracle complexity with either accelerated semi-proximal ADMM or FISTA applied to the dual subproblem as the inner solver. Using semi-proximal ADMM as the inner solver improves the bound to $O(ε^{-2}\log(1/ε))$ under an additional uniform error-bound condition. We further establish convergence of the entire iterate sequence to a KKT point under the same boundedness assumption and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property of the associated potential function. Numerical experiments demonstrate the competitive performance of the proposed method on row-sparse PCA, clustering, robust SVMs, and nonconvex SOCPs.
comment: 59 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
♻ ☆ Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport
Nathan Sauldubois, Xin Zhang
Unlike classical optimal transport, weak transport costs depend nonlinearly on the conditional law of couplings. This feature is essential in problems involving barycenter, conditional moments, and martingale-type constraints. Meanwhile, such conditional dependence makes ordinary Wasserstein geometry insufficient and calls instead for an adapted Wasserstein viewpoint. In this paper, we investigate the entropy-regularized weak optimal transport via gradient flows in adapted Wasserstein space. We derive, from the formal tangent structure of adapted Wasserstein space and the projection onto the set of couplings with prescribed marginals, a coupled McKean--Vlasov SDE. A novel and subtle term is a projection that, at each $Y$-location, averages a weak-transport force that already depends on the conditional law of $Y$ given $X$, thereby preserving marginals while retaining the nonlinear weak-transport structure. Under mild integrability and regularity assumptions, we prove weak existence and uniqueness in law for this projected McKean--Vlasov equation. We then prove that the flow converges, in the adapted Wasserstein topology, to the unique minimizer of the entropic weak optimal transport problem. We also describe a particle approximation and illustrate the dynamics on optimal transport and martingale optimal transport examples.
♻ ☆ Consensus-based optimization with $α$-stable jump processes
Pedro Aceves-Sanchez, Giacomo Albi, Federica Ferrarese, Michael Herty
In this paper, we introduce a CBO method that incorporates jumps driven by an $α$-stable stochastic process within a kinetic framework. This approach naturally induces nonlocal stochastic effects, enhancing the exploration capabilities of the method. We formulate the dynamics at the particle level, providing a detailed description of the associated stochastic system and its asymptotic behavior. In particular, by means of a Fourier-based representation, we derive the corresponding fractional Fokker-Planck equation, which captures the nonlocal diffusion mechanisms generated by $α$-stable processes. As a central result, we establish a rigorous convergence analysis for the proposed method. Finally, we assess its performance through a series of numerical experiments, highlighting the effectiveness of $α$-stable jump dynamics and their advantages over standard diffusion based strategies, especially in complex optimization landscapes.
♻ ☆ A global stochastic maximum principle for delayed forward-backward stochastic control systems
Feng Li
In this paper, we study a delayed forward-backward stochastic control system in which all the coefficients depend on the state and control terms, and the control domain is an arbitrary nonempty set. To handle the terms involving $y$ and $z$ in the second-order expansion, we derive two decompositions of $\big(\hat{y}^\e(\cd), \hat{z}^\e(\cd)\big)$. More precisely, we use the second decomposition to handle the terms involving $f^\e_{yy}, f^\e_{yz}$ and use both decompositions to handle the term involving $f^\e_{zz}$. Finally, a global stochastic maximum principle is obtained.
comment: Substantial revisions, including corrections to the proofs
♻ ☆ Position: Adopt Constraints Over Fixed Penalties in Deep Learning NeurIPS 2026
Juan Ramirez, Meraj Hashemizadeh, Simon Lacoste-Julien
Deep learning models are increasingly subject to explicit requirements, or constraints, such as safety levels, fairness limits, and sparsity budgets. In practice, such requirements are often handled through fixed weighted-sum penalization: the constraints are added to the task loss with fixed coefficients, and the resulting scalarized objective is minimized. This position paper argues that fixed penalization is often ill-suited to deep learning problems with non-negotiable requirements, for three main reasons. First, in non-convex settings, the penalized and constrained problems are not, in general, equivalent, so a minimizer of the penalized objective need not solve the constrained problem. Second, a penalty coefficient sets an objective-constraint trade-off rather than the constraint level, so finding an acceptable coefficient often takes trial and error, each trial a full training run. Third, fixed penalization weakens hard requirements into soft penalties to be traded off against task performance. As a result, compliance is no longer built into the problem, and requirements can be quietly relaxed. We therefore argue that, when a deep learning problem specifies non-negotiable requirements, one should solve the constrained problem itself instead of a surrogate defined by fixed penalization.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track). 10 pages of main text plus appendix; 3 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/merajhashemi/constraints-vs-penalties
♻ ☆ Physics-Informed Neural Networks for coupled stiff transport systems
Laetitia Laguzet, Gabriel Turinici
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) struggle with stiff, regime-changing transport equations due to instability, loss imbalance, and violations of physical consistency. This paper investigates these failures through the Marshak wave equations, a canonical benchmark from radiative transport, where initial and boundary conditions differ by up to 12 orders of magnitude, and proposes modifications to the standard PINN framework to overcome them. Three modifications are introduced: a ScaledSigmoid final activation enforcing physical bounds and positivity of the unknowns; a logarithmic MSE loss replacing the standard quadratic loss for initial and boundary conditions, enabling training across extreme scale disparities; and explicit enforcement of global conservation laws as an additional physics loss term. Monte Carlo sampling with exponential time weighting is used throughout. The proposed framework recovers the Marshak wave dynamics - including the hot, cold, and wave-front regions - in good agreement with a reference Implicit Monte Carlo solution (sub-millimeter absolute error on the front position, although the relative error remains substantial at early times), with run times under 5 minutes. Ablation studies confirm that each ingredient is essential: linear activation, absence of the logarithmic loss, or removal of the PDE term each independently cause the method to fail qualitatively. This work identifies and resolves three concrete failure modes of standard PINN on stiff hyperbolic systems with nonlinear coupling. The combination of bounded activations, scale-aware loss functions, and conservation law enforcement constitutes a framework validated on the present one-dimensional Marshak wave problem, with potential extension to other coupled stiff transport systems in engineering.
♻ ☆ Generalization of Zeroth-Order Method for Quotients of Quadratic Functions
Jonas Bresch
Optimization of quadratic functions and their quotients is relevant in subspace and iterative optimization methods. In this paper, we consider the matrix-free computation of the generalized operator norm and the maximization of a generalized Rayleigh quotient when only forward evaluations of two linear operators $A$ and $B$ are available. The proposed method samples search directions uniformly from the full unit sphere, thereby avoiding tangent-space sampling and explicit access to the metric matrix $B^{\mathrm T}B$. The exact line search along each sampled direction reduces to a $2\times2$ generalized eigenvalue problem on specific Gram matrices. In the generic case its maximizing step has a closed form. We prove that the objective values converge almost surely to the largest generalized eigenvalue and that the distance of the iterates to the leading generalized eigenspace converges to zero. We also relate full-sphere moment estimators to the Riemannian gradient and Hessian. The numerical experiments on synthetic Gaußian operators illustrate the behavior of the methods, and further studies of the proposed algorithms indicate favorable empirical convergence and weak dependence on the tested problem dimensions.
♻ ☆ Analytical benchmark problems and methodological framework for the assessment and comparison of multifidelity optimization methods
L. Mainini, A. Serani, H. Pehlivan, F. Di Fiore, M. P. Rumpfkeil, E. Minisci, D. Quagliarella, S. Yildiz, S. Ficini, R. Pellegrini, A. Thelen, D. Bryson, M. Nikbay, M. Diez, P. Beran
This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmarking framework that includes: (i) a suite of analytical benchmark optimization problems designed to stress-test and validate multifidelity methods; (ii) a set of assessment metrics for quantifying and comparing performance over measurable objectives; and (iii) the classification, evaluation, and comparison of several families of multifidelity optimization methods and frameworks using the proposed benchmarks to identify their respective strengths and weaknesses in real-world scenarios. The proposed benchmark problems are analytically defined functions carefully selected to capture mathematical challenges commonly encountered in real-world applications, including high dimensionality, multimodality, discontinuities, and noise. Their closed-form nature ensures computational efficiency, high reproducibility, and a clear separation of algorithmic behavior from numerical artifacts. The accompanying performance metrics support the systematic evaluation of multifidelity methods, measuring both optimization effectiveness and global approximation accuracy. By providing a rigorous, reproducible, and accessible benchmarking framework, this work aims to enable the broader community to understand, compare, and advance multifidelity optimization methods for complex problems in science and engineering.
♻ ☆ Asynchronous Sensitivity-Based Distributed NMPC
Maximilian Pierer von Esch, Andres Völz, Knut Graichen
This paper presents a cooperative distributed model predictive control (MPC) scheme for nonlinear continuous-time systems. The centralized optimal control problem is solved asynchronously via a fixed number of sensitivity-based distributed programming (SBDP) iterations. The proposed scheme requires only neighbor-to-neighbor communication and no synchronization between agents during optimization. Under nominal MPC stability and bounded information delay, local exponential stability is established for a sufficiently large number of per-agent SBDP iterations. Numerical and hardware-in-the-loop results on both Ethernet and Wi-Fi demonstrate the benefits of an asynchronous execution, reducing execution times by over 60% while maintaining comparable closed loop performance.
♻ ☆ Certified bounds on optimization problems in quantum theory
Younes Naceur, Jie Wang, Victor Magron, Antonio Acín
Semidefinite relaxations of polynomial optimization have become a central tool for addressing the non-convex optimization problems over non-commutative operators that are ubiquitous in quantum information theory and, more in general, quantum physics. Yet, as these global relaxation methods are solved numerically, the bounds issued by the semidefinite solver can - and often do - exceed the global optimum, undermining their certifiability. To counter this issue, we introduce a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds on non-commutative optimization problems from inexact numerical data, and apply it to several paradigmatic problems in quantum information theory. An extension to sparsity and symmetry-adapted semidefinite relaxations is also provided and compared to the general dense scheme. Our results establish rational post-processing as a practical route to reliable certification, pushing semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science.
comment: 30 pages, 11 figures
♻ ☆ Mini-Batch Stochastic Conjugate Gradient Algorithms with Minimal Variance
Caixia Kou, Feifei Gao, Yu-Hong Dai
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods have gained widespread popularity for solving large-scale optimization problems. However, the inherent variance in SGD often leads to slow convergence rates. We introduce a family of unbiased stochastic gradient estimators that encompasses existing estimators from the literature and identify a gradient estimator that not only maintains unbiasedness but also achieves minimal variance. Compared with the existing estimator used in SGD algorithms, the proposed estimator demonstrates a significant reduction in variance. By utilizing this stochastic gradient estimator to approximate the full gradient, we propose two mini-batch stochastic conjugate gradient algorithms with minimal variance. Under the assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness on the objective function, we prove that the two algorithms achieve linear convergence rates. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed gradient estimator in reducing variance and demonstrate that the two stochastic conjugate gradient algorithms exhibit accelerated convergence rates and enhanced stability.
♻ ☆ Gradient Descent's Last Iterate is Often (slightly) Suboptimal
Guy Kornowski, Ohad Shamir
We consider the well-studied setting of minimizing a convex Lipschitz function using either gradient descent (GD) or its stochastic variant (SGD), and examine the last iterate convergence. We prove that $Θ(\sqrt{\log(T)/T})$ is the optimal anytime rate attainable with a fixed stepsize schedule (that does not depend on the total number of steps $T$). The upper bound holds already for SGD, and improves on the $\log(T)/\sqrt{T}$ rate of Shamir and Zhang [2013], as well as the $\sqrt{\log(T)/T}$ rate of Zamani and Glineur [2023] which was proven only for deterministic GD. The matching lower bound holds already for GD, and confirms the conjecture of Jain et al. [2019], namely that the optimal $1/\sqrt{T}$ rate for the last iterate cannot be obtained without prior knowledge of $T$.
comment: Substantially improved version, with new and matching upper and lower bounds
♻ ☆ On the invariance of risk-sensitive LQR gain under input randomization
Yeongjun Jang
This paper shows that the optimal gain of the risk-sensitive linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem is invariant under input randomization when the cost penalizes the realized noisy input. This may appear counterintuitive at first glance because certainty equivalence does not hold for risk-sensitive LQR and input randomization inflates the effective process noise. Nonetheless, the gain is preserved because the input noise enters not only the system dynamics but also the cost functional, and its total effect eventually vanishes. Consequently, the optimal gain and the Riccati recursion need not be recomputed, and the increment in the optimal cost can be readily evaluated in closed form. This result facilitates the use of risk-sensitive LQR in applications that employ input randomization for privacy or exploration, such as dynamic watermarking for replay attack detection.
comment: 6 pages, revised extended version submitted to IEEE L-CSS and ACC 2027, including Section III-F
♻ ☆ A Smoothing Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method with Nonmonotone Backtracking Strategy for Convex Nonsmooth Composite Multiobjective Optimization
Huang Chengzhi
This paper studies convex nonsmooth composite multiobjective optimization problems, whose objectives combine a convex term admitting a smooth approximation with a proper, closed, and convex term. A natural way is to smooth the nonsmooth term and apply proximal gradient method, but reducing the smoothing parameter shrinks step sizes, and solving successive smooth approximations to approach the original solution is computationally expensive. To address this issues, we propose a smoothing accelerated proximal gradient method with nonmonotone backtracking strategy. Each outer iteration starts from a reduced base smoothness estimate, which is increased only if the criterion fails, while the momentum update is linked to the estimate through an exact identity used in the convergence analysis. Under a compact level-set assumption and bounds of parameters, we use merit function to establish rates of $\mathcal{O}(k^{-σ})$, $\mathcal{O}((\log k)/k)$, and $\mathcal{O}(k^{σ-2})$ for different smoothing parameters. Then quasi-Fejér monotonicity yields convergence of the full sequence to a weak Pareto solution. Numerical experiments show that the method can reduce computational cost while preserving high-quality Pareto fronts and examine how the smoothing parameter affects performance.
♻ ☆ Cross-validated feature selection using least-squares support vector machines for binary classification
Masaharu Mori, Shunnosuke Ikeda, Ryuta Tamura, Yuichi Takano, Ryuhei Miyashiro
Support vector machines (SVMs) are widely used for binary classification. However, irrelevant or redundant features can degrade classification accuracy and model interpretability, making feature selection important for SVMs. Most SVM feature selection methods rely on sequential search or regularization and do not directly identify the best feature subset. Mixed-integer optimization (MIO) is a direct approach to best subset selection. Cross-validation (CV) is broadly applicable to feature selection because it evaluates predictive performance on validation data without model assumptions. Although Purcaru et al. (2026) proposed an MIO formulation for CV-based linear-SVM feature selection (SVM-CV), this method suffers from high computational cost. We develop computationally efficient CV-based MIO formulations for feature selection in linear SVM classification by using least squares support vector machines (LS-SVMs). We formulate the problem as a bilevel MIO problem, where the lower-level problem trains LS-SVM classifiers and the upper-level problem selects features based on validation sets. We then reformulate it as a single-level MIO problem by exploiting the optimality conditions of LS-SVM. We propose two formulations: a hinge-loss-based validation model and a least-squares-based validation model. We compare our methods with SVM-CV and other SVM-based and logistic-regression-based methods through simulation experiments on synthetic data. The hinge-loss-based validation model attained high feature selection accuracy under the high-noise and moderate-noise conditions, particularly with more candidate features, and the least-squares-based validation model performed well in feature selection under the low-noise condition at the lower correlation level. Furthermore, our two models achieved substantially faster computation than the existing SVM-CV model.

♻ ☆ PREFER: Personalized Review Summarization with Online Preference Learning
Millend Roy, Agostino Capponi, Vineet Goyal
Product reviews significantly influence purchasing decisions on e-commerce platforms. However, the sheer volume of reviews can overwhelm users, obscuring information most relevant to their individual needs. Existing e-commerce summarization systems typically produce generic, static summaries that fail to account for the fact that (i) different users prioritize different product characteristics, and (ii) these preferences may evolve with interactions. To address these challenges, we propose an online learning framework that generates personalized summaries for each user by representing user interests in a latent aspect space and selecting preference-aligned review evidence. Our system then iteratively refines its understanding of user preferences by incorporating feedback on the generated summaries directly over time. We evaluate our framework on Amazon Reviews'23 using controlled feedback simulations and robustness checks with held-out-history, independent-embedding, and external LLM-based evaluators. These experiments show improvements in preference-aligned evidence selection under the evaluated feedback settings. A separate human-based study finds that scenario-conditioned summaries are preferred over generic (uniformly-aggregated) alternatives in 69.9% of paired comparisons.
♻ ☆ Polyhedral Outer Approximation for MISOCP: Geometry and Progressive Integrality
Yongzheng Dai
Polyhedral outer approximation (OA) is widely used to solve mixed-integer second-order cone programs (MISOCPs) by iteratively strengthening polyhedral relaxations of conic constraints. However, the accumulation of cutting planes can increase the difficulty of solving the resulting mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), while repeatedly solving these MILPs can be computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we investigate the geometry of supporting cuts and the computational role of integrality in OA. First, we establish theoretical bounds showing that the marginal contribution of a new supporting cut decreases at least linearly as its supporting direction approaches an existing one. Motivated by this analysis, we develop a closed-form cut-generation strategy that balances separation depth and directional diversity. Second, we propose a progressive-integrality OA framework that strengthens the polyhedral approximation through linear programs and partially integral relaxations before solving full MILPs. We theoretically characterize the transfer of cut-induced bound improvements across integrality levels and provide a branch-and-bound interpretation of the framework. Computational experiments on CBLIB instances and large-scale AC unit-commitment models demonstrate substantial improvements over classical OA and direct MISOCP solution, with runtime reductions of up to 62\% relative to classical OA on the reported power-system instances.

João Sousa-Pinto, Dominique Orban
We present a parallel solver for finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) problems with arbitrary stagewise linear equality constraints, using linear work and logarithmic depth in the horizon for fixed local dimensions. The solver uses a two-part reduction that separates feasibility from optimization. First, an associative suffix scan computes the states from which each remaining horizon is feasible. Second, we use these feasible-continuation sets to eliminate the constraints independently at each stage, producing an unconstrained LQR problem with smaller or equal, possibly stage-varying dimensions. A parallel unconstrained-LQR solver completes the primal solution. Finally, we recover valid multipliers from the original KKT stationarity equations using a logarithmic-depth contraction-expansion procedure, even when the multipliers are not unique. Sequential and parallel implementations are validated against dense KKT solutions and original residuals. We release a C++/CUDA implementation with JAX bindings under the MIT license.

♻ ☆ Uniqueness and reconstruction of reciprocal constitutive generators from equilibrium response maps
Jonathan Washburn, Megan Simons
We recover a shared constitutive generator from equilibrium locations on weighted graphs. For an even $C^2$ log-coordinate potential with positive curvature, the complete two-site response map determines the generator up to positive scale. A sweep over all positive boundary values at one fixed, possibly unknown, unequal weight ratio gives global identification through a Schröder-Koenigs iteration. We extend this result to a three-vertex chain with two observed free vertices under a sweep condition. For variable-ratio control, we prove finite-target recovery, local Lipschitz stability, and noisy-bisection bounds. Fixed-ratio stability and nonparametric estimation under uncertain controls remain open. In the reciprocal family $J_p$, an exact Gaussian model-selection probability benchmarks synthetic experiments under observation noise and errors in variables. These are identifiability results under controls; no measured data or physical system is analyzed.

♻ ☆ The Global Empirical NTK: Self-Referential Bias and Dimensionality of Gradient Descent Learning
James Hazelden, Laura Driscoll, Eli Shlizerman, Eric Shea-Brown
In training a neural network with gradient descent (GD), each iteration induces a linear operator that governs the first-order updates to a model's internal state variables. We call this operator the Global Empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (GeNTK). In finite-width networks, GeNTK is typically intractable to form, leading prior work to focus on restrictive settings, such as tracking only outputs or infinite-width limits. Here, we bridge this gap by studying the structure of GeNTK across many models. Formulating the model state as the solution to a global implicit constraint, we derive GeNTK as a product of two operators: K, accounting for immediate parameter-to-state interactions, and P, describing internal state-to-state dependencies. For a broad class of "weight-based models", such as RNNs and transformers, we prove a universal Kronecker-core theorem showing that K admits an exact, forward-pass-computable form given by the Gram matrix of weight-site variables. This core gives a measurable state-dependent restriction on Euclidean GD, termed "self-referential bias": current activity filters which adjoint directions can drive a first-order update. For recurrent models (GRUs and RNNs), we examine the spectrum of GeNTK and formalize notions of low-rank, biased learning in terms of reduced spatial or temporal ranks of the full operator. Practically, this explains why some RNN initializations yield better learning, while some plateau, by biasing the GeNTK and thus restricting learning to a small domain of learnable tasks. To demonstrate computational viability, we validate the main theorems in a self-attention transformer and a pretrained Pythia transformer language model with 410 million parameters. Overall, our results expose tractable local rank and mode-selective biases in the finite-width GD geometry and open the door to principled study of the GeNTK, a bridge between theory and practice.

♻ ☆ Learning to Control: The iUzawa-Net for Nonsmooth Optimal Control of Linear PDEs
Yongcun Song, Xiaoming Yuan, Hangrui Yue, Tianyou Zeng
We propose an optimization-informed deep neural network approach, named iUzawa-Net, aiming for the first solver that enables real-time solutions for a class of nonsmooth optimal control problems of linear partial differential equations (PDEs). The iUzawa-Net unrolls an inexact Uzawa method for saddle point problems, replacing classical preconditioners and PDE solvers with specifically designed learnable neural networks. We prove universal approximation properties and establish the asymptotic $\varepsilon$-optimality for the iUzawa-Net, and validate its promising numerical efficiency through nonsmooth elliptic and parabolic optimal control problems. Our techniques offer a versatile framework for designing and analyzing various optimization-informed deep learning approaches to optimal control and other PDE-constrained optimization problems. The proposed learning-to-control approach synergizes model-based optimization algorithms and data-driven deep learning techniques, inheriting the merits of both methodologies.

♻ ☆ A polynomial-time solvable class of sparse box-constrained polynomial optimization problems
Aida Khajavirad
We study the problem of minimizing a multivariate polynomial function over the unit hypercube. Exploiting sparsity in the interaction graph or hypergraph, we identify variables that can be restricted to binary values and eliminate the remaining continuous variables component-wise, reducing the problem to structured binary polynomial optimization. For quadratic objectives, we obtain polynomial-time solvability in the standard Turing model under conditions on treewidth and a nonconvexity measure of the continuous components. For higher-degree objectives, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm in the unit-cost algebraic RAM model under logarithmic incidence treewidth and small, weakly coupled continuous components.
♻ ☆ Data-Driven Maintenance Optimization: Aligning Prognostic Learning with Decision Objective
